title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 75–76
description: Advanced ways to praise, compliment, flatter and recognise achievement; promises, solemn commitments, betting expressions, odds and figurative risk.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal vocabulary study from the user-provided book. Vocabulary targets were chosen after examining the unit pages, exercises and answer key; translations, examples and usage notes are independently written and do not reproduce textbook exercises or passages.

audit.scope: Teaching sections A–B, warning and language-help boxes, exercises 75.1–75.5 and 76.1–76.4, and corresponding answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is used only for selected individual words where sufficiently confident. Empty IPA avoids unverified or misleading connected-speech transcription.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing content and metadata are English except Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Checked original teaching pages, exercises and answer key; wrote original examples and concise contrast notes; performed JSON schema, ID, provenance, audio-target and source-page static checks against the canonical reference.
audit.limitations: No audio recordings are included; live VocabLab import, browser TTS output and pronunciation recognition have not been tested. Register and dialect differences are explained in relevant notes.

units.title: Unit 75 — A pat on the back: complimenting and praising
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 156–157 (PDF pages 158–159).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
learningObjectives: Select collocations for offering, receiving and interpreting compliments, including ambivalent compliments.
Distinguish public acclaim and formal praise from informal or self-serving flattery.
Use compliment on, praise for, extol the virtues of, and other fixed patterns accurately.
Recognise word families and register contrasts among laudatory, laudable, obsequious and smarmy.

sectionsChecked: A · Collocations with compliment and praise
B · Other expressions relating to praising

items.example: The supervisor paid the junior researcher a compliment on her clear presentation.
items.note: Pay someone a compliment is an established expression; do not say give someone a compliment in every context.

items.pt: fazer algo para receber elogios; buscar elogios indiretamente
items.example: He kept mentioning his new award, clearly fishing for compliments.
items.note: Suggests seeking praise rather than asking for it directly; often mildly critical.

items.example: I chose to take her remark as a compliment rather than an insult.
items.note: Take something as a compliment describes the interpretation of another person’s remark.

items.pt: um elogio com crítica disfarçada; elogio venenoso
items.example: Calling her remarkably articulate for someone so young was a back-handed compliment.
items.note: It sounds positive on the surface but carries a deliberate slight or criticism.

items.pt: um elogio ambíguo; elogio com dois sentidos
items.example: He gave me a double-edged compliment by saying my report was excellent for a first attempt.
items.note: Combines praise with an unintended negative implication; contrasts with a deliberately malicious back-handed compliment.

items.example: The examiner complimented her on the precision of her reasoning.
items.note: Use compliment someone on something or on doing something; the preposition on is required.

items.example: The congregation gathered to give praise to God.
items.note: The book notes that this construction is particularly common in religious language.

items.example: Her decision to publish the negative findings was praiseworthy.
items.note: Adjective for conduct or achievements deserving praise.

items.example: The manager praised the team for identifying the fault before deployment.
items.note: Praise someone for a contribution or for doing something; not praise someone of.

items.pt: muito elogiado; amplamente reconhecido por sua qualidade
items.example: The new translation was highly praised for its clarity and elegance.
items.note: Highly intensifies the degree of praise; commonly used in reviews.

items.pt: elogiado por muita gente; amplamente elogiado
items.example: The initiative was widely praised by independent researchers.
items.note: Widely emphasises the range or number of people giving praise, rather than intensity alone.

items.example: The reviewers praised the stage design to the skies.
items.note: An emphatic idiom meaning praise very enthusiastically.

items.pt: exaltar as qualidades de; fazer muitos elogios a
items.example: Several former students sang the praises of the new mentoring programme.
items.note: Sing the praises of someone or something is idiomatic, often with enthusiastic approval.
items.speechText: sing the praises of our team

items.example: After the performance, the judges showered praise on the young soloist.
items.note: A vivid expression for giving a great deal of praise; heap praise on is similar.

items.example: The reviewers heaped praise on the director for the restrained ending.
items.note: A strong accumulation metaphor: praise is given in large quantities.

items.pt: desmerecer com um elogio sem entusiasmo
items.example: Saying the applicant was reasonably punctual damned her with faint praise.
items.note: Apparent praise is so weak that it conveys disapproval.

items.example: Her unexpected compliment made the new volunteer feel welcome.
items.note: A compliment is a positive remark; do not confuse with complement, which means something that completes or enhances.

items.example: Her contribution to the project deserves genuine praise.
items.note: Can be a noun or a verb; praise is generally uncountable when it refers to approval.

items.pt: prestar homenagem a; reconhecer publicamente as contribuições de
items.example: The conference opened with a speech paying tribute to the late physicist.
items.note: Usually more formal than praise; particularly appropriate in public acknowledgements.

items.example: The audience gave the orchestra a standing ovation after the final movement.
items.note: A prolonged round of applause with the audience on its feet.

items.pt: aplaudir de pé; fazer uma ovação de pé
items.example: The delegates gave the retiring director a standing ovation.
items.note: The conventional verb is give; the object is the person or group being applauded.

items.pt: enaltecer as virtudes de; exaltar as qualidades de
items.example: The brochure extols the virtues of travelling outside the peak season.
items.note: Formal and sometimes promotional; extol means praise enthusiastically.
items.speechText: extol the virtues of the new approach

items.example: The presenter extolled the benefits of open access to scientific data.
items.note: A formal collocation especially common in persuasive writing or speeches.

items.pt: a pessoa mais celebrada de; sensação de
items.example: Following her breakthrough novel, she became the toast of the literary world.
items.note: Describes somebody widely celebrated for a recent success, often in the arts or media.

items.pt: um reconhecimento; um elogio pelo esforço
items.example: Completing the project ahead of schedule earned the team a pat on the back.
items.note: Often metaphorical, meaning praise for an achievement rather than an actual touch.

items.pt: parabenizar alguém; dar um tapinha nas costas
items.example: The coach patted the players on the back for their determination.
items.note: May be literal or figurative; often describes encouraging recognition.

items.example: The documentary earned plaudits for its careful treatment of a complex subject.
items.note: Formal expression; plaudits are enthusiastic praise or approval.

items.example: Her research won plaudits from specialists in several disciplines.
items.note: Similar to earn plaudits; especially common in journalism and reviews.

items.example: The production received plaudits from critics across the country.
items.note: Plural noun commonly found in formal arts and review contexts.

items.example: The panel lauded the engineers for their commitment to safety.
items.note: A formal verb meaning praise strongly, often in official statements.

items.example: Reducing waste is a laudable aim, even if the proposed method is flawed.
items.note: Describes an action, objective or motive that deserves approval.

items.example: The scientist received a laudatory introduction from the conference chair.
items.note: Describes a remark, speech or review containing high praise.

items.example: He flattered the chairperson in the hope of securing an invitation.
items.note: May suggest insincere praise motivated by self-interest, but can also refer to making someone look attractive.

items.example: He tried to make up to the influential investor before the meeting.
items.note: Informal, chiefly British; denotes ingratiating behaviour.

items.pt: puxar o saco de; bajular servilmente
items.example: He was willing to crawl to senior managers to win promotion.
items.note: Informal and strongly disapproving; suggests exaggerated submissiveness.

items.example: Nobody respected his habit of sucking up to powerful colleagues.
items.note: Informal and critical; common in spoken English.

items.pt: puxar o saco do chefe; bajular de forma servil
items.example: She refused to lick the boss’s boots merely to get a favourable appraisal.
items.note: A specific, naturally pronounceable version of the idiom lick someone’s boots.

items.pt: bajulador e afetado; meloso de forma interesseira
items.example: His smarmy compliments made the interview panel uncomfortable.
items.note: Informal, negative adjective implying insincere and ingratiating behaviour.

items.pt: falso e bajulador; escorregadio no trato
items.example: Her colleague’s slimy attempts to win favour were obvious to everyone.
items.note: Informal, strongly disapproving when used about character; literally also means covered in slime.

items.example: The staff disliked the new assistant because he behaved like a crawler.
items.note: An insulting informal noun for someone who flatters authority figures.

items.pt: um bajulador; uma pessoa que faz elogios interesseiros
items.example: She is too experienced to be deceived by an obvious flatterer.
items.note: More neutral than crawler, although the behaviour may still be viewed negatively.

items.example: The adviser’s servile tone undermined the independence of his judgement.
items.note: Formal, negative adjective for excessive deference or obedience.

items.pt: subserviente e bajulador; obsequioso em excesso
items.example: The executive was surrounded by obsequious assistants who never challenged his decisions.
items.note: Formal, strongly negative term for excessive, self-serving politeness.

items.pt: valorizar a silhueta; cair bem no corpo
items.example: The tailored jacket flatters her figure without being too formal.
items.note: Here flatter is positive and means make somebody look more attractive, not give false verbal praise.

items.example: She recognised the proposal as flattery rather than an objective assessment.
items.note: Uncountable noun for excessive or insincere praise.

items.pt: bajulação não vai adiantar; puxar o saco não resolve
items.example: Flattery will get you nowhere; the committee will judge only the evidence.
items.note: Fixed response rejecting someone’s attempt to influence through praise.

items.example: The referees were complimentary about the quality of her writing.
items.note: Exercise-linked adjective from compliment; do not confuse with complimentary meaning free of charge.

items.example: Her supervisor made a complimentary remark about the clarity of the diagrams.
items.note: This adjective can mean praising; in other contexts complimentary may mean provided free.

units.title: Unit 76 — Promises and bets
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 158–159 (PDF pages 160–161).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish literal promises, solemn oaths and expressions of expected future potential.
Use vow, pledge, resolution and swear with appropriate register and grammatical complements.
Interpret formal and informal betting vocabulary in literal and figurative senses.
Apply idioms such as go back on your word, hedge your bets and the odds are against accurately.

items.pt: prometer o mundo a alguém; fazer promessas exageradas
items.example: The candidate promised voters the earth without explaining how he would fund the plans.
items.note: Often implies that the promises are unrealistic or unlikely to be fulfilled.

items.pt: prometer o impossível; prometer mundos e fundos
items.example: The salesman promised us the moon, but the product barely worked.
items.note: An alternative to promise someone the earth; usually critical.

items.pt: prometer ser; dar sinais de que será
items.example: The upcoming exhibition promises to be a highlight of the festival.
items.note: In this sense, promise means show signs that something will happen, not make a commitment.

items.example: We anticipate a substantial rise in applications next term.
items.note: More formal than expect; does not necessarily imply looking forward positively.

items.example: The young composer shows great promise despite having little formal training.
items.note: Promise here is a noun describing potential for future success.

items.example: Preliminary findings are promising, although further trials are needed.
items.note: Adjective describing potential for a favourable outcome.

items.example: Before giving evidence, the witness took an oath to tell the truth.
items.note: A solemn or formal promise, particularly in legal settings.

items.example: The new officials were required to swear an oath before taking office.
items.note: Swear can mean make a solemn promise or use offensive language, depending on context.

items.example: The witness gave her testimony under oath.
items.note: Legal expression indicating an obligation to tell the truth.

items.example: Every witness must swear to tell the truth before answering the court’s questions.
items.note: Swear to do something means make a solemn commitment.

items.pt: eu tinha certeza absoluta; eu jurava que
items.example: I could have sworn the deadline was Friday, not Thursday.
items.note: Informal expression of strong but possibly mistaken recollection.

items.pt: não posso afirmar com absoluta certeza
items.example: I think the meeting starts at nine, but I couldn’t swear to it.
items.note: Signals uncertainty despite having a tentative belief.

items.pt: recomendar com muita convicção; confiar plenamente em
items.example: My grandfather swears by this traditional recipe for bread.
items.note: Means strongly believe in the effectiveness of something; not make an oath.

items.example: The editor removed several swear words from the televised interview.
items.note: Refers to taboo or offensive words; the other major sense of swear is make an oath.

items.example: The programme carries a warning because it contains bad language.
items.note: A more general expression for offensive speech; may include swearing.

items.example: The university pledged additional support for students affected by the cuts.
items.note: Formal and frequent in institutional, political and fundraising contexts; both noun and verb.

items.pt: fazer um voto ou juramento solene; voto
items.example: The campaigners vowed to continue until the law was reviewed.
items.note: A determined or solemn promise, especially in written reports; both noun and verb.

items.example: The couple exchanged vows in a small ceremony by the sea.
items.note: Commonly refers to promises made during a marriage ceremony.

items.pt: uma resolução de Ano-Novo; promessa de mudança
items.example: Her New Year’s resolution was to spend less time checking her phone.
items.note: Typically a commitment to change behaviour at the start of a year.

items.pt: virar a página; mudar de comportamento para melhor
items.example: After failing the course, he decided to turn over a new leaf and study consistently.
items.note: Idiomatic expression for making a fresh start with improved behaviour.

items.pt: tomar uma resolução; firmar um propósito
items.example: She made a resolution to exercise regularly throughout the year.
items.note: Make a resolution is standard; resolutions may later be kept or broken.

items.example: The organisation kept its promise to publish the results openly.
items.note: Keep contrasts with break a promise or go back on your word.

items.pt: quebrar uma promessa; não cumprir o prometido
items.example: He broke his promise to return the equipment before the inspection.
items.note: Used for not honouring an undertaking.

items.pt: voltar atrás no que prometeu; faltar com a palavra
items.example: The contractor went back on his word after the price had been agreed.
items.note: An idiom emphasising a breach of trust or commitment.

items.example: The judge had the witness put on oath before questioning began.
items.note: A legal formulation; be put under oath is another established expression.

items.pt: um compromisso formal; uma promessa solene
items.example: The charity received a pledge of additional funding from a local business.
items.note: Noun related to pledge as a verb; often relates to money, loyalty or public commitments.

items.example: He made a vow never to conceal important results again.
items.note: Noun related to vow; especially common with determined personal decisions and marriage.

items.example: She bet a small sum on the result of the match.
items.note: As a noun or verb, involves risking something on an uncertain outcome; also used figuratively.

items.pt: jogo de apostas; prática de apostar dinheiro
items.example: His research examines the social effects of gambling.
items.note: The act of risking money on uncertain outcomes; broader than a single bet.

items.example: The stake was modest, but the possible loss still mattered to him.
items.note: Here a stake is the amount placed at risk; a different sense occurs in at stake.

items.example: They staked money on a result they could not predict with confidence.
items.note: Stake something on an outcome means risk it, especially money.

items.example: The safety of thousands of residents is at stake in this decision.
items.note: Frequently figurative: the outcome could cause something important to be lost.

items.example: I would wager that the committee will reject such a vague proposal.
items.note: More formal than bet; used both for literal betting and confident predictions.

items.pt: sua melhor opção; escolha mais segura
items.example: Your best bet is to contact the admissions office before submitting the form.
items.note: An informal recommendation; no actual monetary bet is involved.

items.pt: não conte com isso; duvido que aconteça
items.example: Will the repairs be finished by tomorrow? Don’t bet on it.
items.note: Informal response expressing doubt about a prediction.

items.pt: fazer uma aposta pequena e ocasional
items.example: My aunt occasionally has a flutter on a horse race.
items.note: Chiefly British, informal; refers to a small recreational bet.

items.pt: apostar dinheiro em; apostar que algo vai acontecer
items.example: I’d put money on the proposal being rejected in its current form.
items.note: May refer to a literal bet or figuratively to strong confidence.

items.pt: apostar minha vida que; ter certeza absoluta de
items.example: I’d bet my life on her recognising the error before the meeting.
items.note: Strong idiomatic assertion of confidence; not normally a literal risk to one’s life.

items.example: Can we include your name among the volunteers? You bet!
items.note: An enthusiastic informal affirmation, especially common in North American English.

items.pt: distribuir os riscos; não apostar tudo numa única opção
items.example: Rather than relying on one supplier, the company hedged its bets by signing two smaller contracts.
items.note: Reduce risk by keeping several options open; usually figurative.

items.pt: as probabilidades; as chances de algo acontecer
items.example: The odds of meeting the deadline improved after the team received help.
items.note: Refers to statistical or betting chances; use odds of with a noun or -ing form.

items.pt: as chances estão contra; é pouco provável
items.example: The odds are against the project securing funding this year.
items.note: Suggests an unfavourable probability; typically followed by a noun or -ing clause.

items.word: the odds are in favour of
items.pt: as probabilidades favorecem; é mais provável que
items.example: With such extensive preparation, the odds are in favour of a successful launch.
items.note: Contrasts with the odds are against; British spelling favour.
items.speechText: the odds are in favour of success

items.example: The wager was settled as soon as the match finished.
items.note: Noun equivalent of bet, with a more formal flavour.
